row.story:
Sun glittered on the allotment greenhouse. Mara arrived with a waxed paper parcel of replacement beans. She had forgotten Ivo's watering, then blamed the tap. She wanted her friend back. At the gate she shifted the stone jamming its foot, pulled it open and carried the parcel up the path.

"Can I come in?" Mara asked. Ivo lifted his bucket away from the doorway. "Mind the latch." She opened the door, carried the parcel inside and put it on the dry bench before shutting the door. The dead bean stalks stood in their row. He had not thrown them away yet.

"The beans are for you," Mara said. Ivo left the string alone. "Did the shop have a tap too?" Her prepared excuses deserted her. "I forgot. The tap worked. Then I lied." He pressed a thumb into the bench soil. "I spent an hour taking it apart." This time she did not explain herself away.

The greenhouse had grown close and breathless. Ivo's young tomatoes drooped towards the hot bench. He pulled the vent cord, but the cord parted and the pane stayed shut. Mara watched a leaf curl against the glass. "It has to stay open," Ivo said. "Not just while someone stands here holding it."

Mara tried to lift the tomato tray, but its rotten wooden base sagged. She set it back before it broke. As the heat curled the leaves, she slid her parcel under the bench instead. By the time she looked up, the stems had collapsed. The replacement beans were protected. Ivo's tomatoes were not.

Ivo looked at the collapsed tomatoes. "Not another tray today," he said. Mara spread the beans in his open sandwich tin and put it on the shelf. "I can come back and help clear up." He paused. "Saturday. While I am here." She left the tin open. There was work to return for, not a harvest to claim.

They stepped onto the path and Mara closed the door. Ivo kept the key. "Knock on Saturday." She nodded without asking for it. Through the glass stood an open tin of unsown beans. There would be no coming and going on her own yet. She waited until he had finished speaking before turning towards the gate.

row.story:
Wind rattled the allotment greenhouse. Mara arrived with a waxed paper parcel of replacement beans. She had forgotten Ivo's watering, then blamed the tap. She wanted her friend back. At the gate she shifted the stone jamming its foot, pulled it open and carried the parcel up the path.

Mara pushed the parcel towards him. "The tap must have stuck. These should replace them." Ivo pushed it back. "I checked the tap. There was nothing wrong with it." She kept her hands beside the parcel instead of answering. Between them the string lay in a neat bow, still untied.

A gust lifted the roof vent. Rain blew through the gap onto Ivo's young tomatoes, bending the matchstick stems. He pulled the closing cord; it came away in his hand. Mara caught the swinging end. Neither pull had moved the vent. "We need to hold it down," he said, looking up at the next cloud.

Mara tested the repair roll. Enough tape remained. Ivo held the vent down while she taped its handle to the bracket. She used the last length and set the empty roll down. When they let go, rain stopped striking the tray. The parcel was still on the bench, its bow untouched; for once it had not been the answer.

Ivo gathered the beans from the parcel she opened and tipped them into Mara's cupped hands. "They are yours. I did not ask for replacements." She looked at the small hard shapes. "I helped, though." He nodded towards the vent. "That was help. It wasn't an answer about the tap."

Mara stepped outside, shut the door and walked back to the open gate with the beans in her hands. The empty waxed paper stayed on his bench. Ivo stayed by the greenhouse. She had brought something to leave behind and was carrying the important part away. At the gate she put the beans in her pocket, one careful handful at a time.

"The beans are for you," Mara said. Ivo left the string alone. "Did the shop have a tap too?" Her prepared excuses deserted her. "I forgot. The tap worked. Then I lied." He pressed a thumb into the bench soil. "I spent an hour taking it apart." This time she did not explain herself away.

A gust lifted the roof vent. Rain blew through the gap onto Ivo's young tomatoes, bending the matchstick stems. He pulled the closing cord; it came away in his hand. Mara caught the swinging end. Neither pull had moved the vent. "We need to hold it down," he said, looking up at the next cloud.

The tape roll was empty. Mara showed Ivo the cardboard centre, then asked for his sandwich tin. He opened it. She untied the parcel, tipped the beans into the tin, and spread the waxed paper across the gap and tied it against the vent handle with the parcel string. The tomatoes were sheltered now; her present had become a piece of the greenhouse.

Mara took the dry beans from the sandwich tin. Ivo moved six empty pots towards her and kept six for himself. "You can take a turn again," he said. "But tell me if you cannot come." They pressed a bean into each pot. She left the soil loose this time, watching how lightly his fingers moved.

Outside, Mara closed the greenhouse door. Ivo put the spare key in her palm. "This does not make last week disappear." "I know." Through the glass they could see twelve dark circles of watered soil. The paper patch breathed above the pots. She closed her hand around the key, not the beans.

"Can I come in?" Mara asked. Ivo lifted his bucket away from the doorway. "Mind the latch." She opened the door, carried the parcel inside and put it on the dry bench before shutting the door. The dead bean stalks stood in their row. He had not thrown them away yet.

"The beans are for you," Mara said. Ivo left the string alone. "Did the shop have a tap too?" Her prepared excuses deserted her. "I forgot. The tap worked. Then I lied." He pressed a thumb into the bench soil. "I spent an hour taking it apart." This time she did not explain herself away.

The greenhouse had grown close and breathless. Ivo's young tomatoes drooped towards the hot bench. He pulled the vent cord, but the cord parted and the pane stayed shut. Mara watched a leaf curl against the glass. "It has to stay open," Ivo said. "Not just while someone stands here holding it."

The tape roll was empty. Mara showed Ivo the cardboard centre, then asked for his sandwich tin. He opened it. She untied the parcel, tipped the beans into the tin, and folded the waxed paper into a thick wedge and tied the raised vent handle to its bracket with the parcel string. The tomatoes were sheltered now; her present had become a piece of the greenhouse.

Mara took the dry beans from the sandwich tin. Ivo moved six empty pots towards her and kept six for himself. "Only while I am here," he said. Mara nodded and stayed beside him. They pressed a bean into each pot. She left the soil loose this time, watching how lightly his fingers moved.

They stepped onto the path and Mara closed the door. Ivo kept the key. "Knock on Saturday." She nodded without asking for it. Through the glass stood twelve newly filled pots. There would be no coming and going on her own yet. She waited until he had finished speaking before turning towards the gate.

"I wanted to make it right." He looked at the fallen tomatoes. "You saved the present. I wanted you to tell me the truth."

She had brought something to leave behind and was carrying the important part away. At the gate she put the beans in her pocket, one careful handful at a time.

"The beans are for you," Mara said. Ivo left the string alone. "Did the shop have a tap too?" Her prepared excuses deserted her. "I forgot. The tap worked. Then I lied." He pressed a thumb into the bench soil. "I spent an hour taking it apart." This time she did not explain herself away.

The greenhouse had grown close and breathless. Ivo's young tomatoes drooped towards the hot bench. He pulled the vent cord, but the cord parted and the pane stayed shut. Mara watched a leaf curl against the glass. "It has to stay open," Ivo said. "Not just while someone stands here holding it."

Mara tested the repair roll. Enough tape remained. Ivo held the vent up while she bound its handle to the upper bracket. She used the last length and set the empty roll down. When they let go, cooler air reached the tray. The parcel was still on the bench, its bow untouched; for once it had not been the answer.

Mara took the dry beans from the parcel she opened. Ivo moved six empty pots towards her and kept six for himself. "You can take a turn again," he said. "But tell me if you cannot come." They pressed a bean into each pot. She left the soil loose this time, watching how lightly his fingers moved.

Outside, Mara closed the greenhouse door. Ivo put the spare key in her palm. "This does not make last week disappear." "I know." Through the glass they could see twelve dark circles of watered soil. Above the pots, the repaired vent held steady. She closed her hand around the key, not the beans.

Wind rattled the allotment greenhouse. Mara arrived with a waxed paper parcel of replacement beans. She had forgotten Ivo's watering, then blamed the tap. She wanted her friend back. At the gate she shifted the stone jamming its foot, pulled it open and carried the parcel up the path.

A gust lifted the roof vent. Rain blew through the gap onto Ivo's young tomatoes, bending the matchstick stems. He pulled the closing cord; it came away in his hand. Mara caught the swinging end. Neither pull had moved the vent. "We need to hold it down," he said, looking up at the next cloud.

Mara tested the repair roll. Enough tape remained. Ivo held the vent down while she taped its handle to the bracket. She used the last length and set the empty roll down. When they let go, rain stopped striking the tray. The parcel was still on the bench, its bow untouched; for once it had not been the answer.

Ivo gathered the beans from the parcel she opened and tipped them into Mara's cupped hands. "They are yours. I did not ask for replacements." She looked at the small hard shapes. "I helped, though." He nodded towards the vent. "That was help. It wasn't an answer about the tap."

Mara stepped outside, shut the door and walked back to the open gate with the beans in her hands. The empty waxed paper stayed on his bench. Ivo stayed by the greenhouse. She had brought something to leave behind and was carrying the important part away. At the gate she put the beans in her pocket, one careful handful at a time.

"The beans are for you," Mara said. Ivo left the string alone. "Did the shop have a tap too?" Her prepared excuses deserted her. "I forgot. The tap worked. Then I lied." He pressed a thumb into the bench soil. "I spent an hour taking it apart." This time she did not explain herself away.

A gust lifted the roof vent. Rain blew through the gap onto Ivo's young tomatoes, bending the matchstick stems. He pulled the closing cord; it came away in his hand. Mara caught the swinging end. Neither pull had moved the vent. "We need to hold it down," he said, looking up at the next cloud.

Mara tried to lift the tomato tray, but its rotten wooden base sagged. She set it back before it broke. As the wind shook the leaves, she slid her parcel under the bench instead. By the time she looked up, the stems had collapsed. The replacement beans were protected. Ivo's tomatoes were not.

Ivo looked at the collapsed tomatoes. "Not another tray today," he said. Mara spread the beans in his open sandwich tin and put it on the shelf. "I can come back and help clear up." He paused. "Saturday. While I am here." She left the tin open. There was work to return for, not a harvest to claim.

They stepped onto the path and Mara closed the door. Ivo kept the key. "Knock on Saturday." She nodded without asking for it. Through the glass stood an open tin of unsown beans. There would be no coming and going on her own yet. She waited until he had finished speaking before turning towards the gate.

"Can I come in?" Mara asked. Ivo lifted his bucket away from the doorway. "Mind the latch." She opened the door, carried the parcel inside and put it on the dry bench before shutting the door. The dead bean stalks stood in their row. He had not thrown them away yet.

"The beans are for you," Mara said. Ivo left the string alone. "Did the shop have a tap too?" Her prepared excuses deserted her. "I forgot. The tap worked. Then I lied." He pressed a thumb into the bench soil. "I spent an hour taking it apart." This time she did not explain herself away.

The greenhouse had grown close and breathless. Ivo's young tomatoes drooped towards the hot bench. He pulled the vent cord, but the cord parted and the pane stayed shut. Mara watched a leaf curl against the glass. "It has to stay open," Ivo said. "Not just while someone stands here holding it."

Mara tested the repair roll. Enough tape remained. Ivo held the vent up while she bound its handle to the upper bracket. She used the last length and set the empty roll down. When they let go, cooler air reached the tray. The parcel was still on the bench, its bow untouched; for once it had not been the answer.

Mara took the dry beans from the parcel she opened. Ivo moved six empty pots towards her and kept six for himself. "You can take a turn again," he said. "But tell me if you cannot come." They pressed a bean into each pot. She left the soil loose this time, watching how lightly his fingers moved.

Outside, Mara closed the greenhouse door. Ivo put the spare key in her palm. "This does not make last week disappear." "I know." Through the glass they could see twelve dark circles of watered soil. Above the pots, the repaired vent held steady. She closed her hand around the key, not the beans.

Mara tried to lift the tomato tray, but its rotten wooden base sagged. She set it back before it broke. As the heat curled the leaves, she slid her parcel under the bench instead. By the time she looked up, the stems had collapsed. The replacement beans were protected. Ivo's tomatoes were not.

Ivo looked at the collapsed tomatoes. "Not another tray today," he said. Mara spread the beans in his open sandwich tin and put it on the shelf. "I can come back and help clear up." He paused. "Saturday. While I am here." She left the tin open. There was work to return for, not a harvest to claim.

They stepped onto the path and Mara closed the door. Ivo kept the key. "Knock on Saturday." She nodded without asking for it. Through the glass stood an open tin of unsown beans. There would be no coming and going on her own yet. She waited until he had finished speaking before turning towards the gate.

Mara pushed the parcel towards him. "The tap must have stuck. These should replace them." Ivo pushed it back. "I checked the tap. There was nothing wrong with it." She kept her hands beside the parcel instead of answering. Between them the string lay in a neat bow, still untied.

She untied the parcel, tipped the beans into the tin, and spread the waxed paper across the gap and tied it against the vent handle with the parcel string. The tomatoes were sheltered now; her present had become a piece of the greenhouse.

Ivo gathered the beans from the tin and tipped them into Mara's cupped hands. "They are yours. I did not ask for replacements." She looked at the small hard shapes. "I helped, though." He nodded towards the vent. "That was help. It wasn't an answer about the tap."

Mara stepped outside, shut the door and walked back to the open gate with the beans in her hands. Her waxed paper stayed in the vent. Ivo stayed by the greenhouse. She had brought something to leave behind and was carrying the important part away. At the gate she put the beans in her pocket, one careful handful at a time.

"Can I come in?" Mara asked. Ivo lifted his bucket away from the doorway. "Mind the latch." She opened the door, carried the parcel inside and put it on the dry bench before shutting the door. The dead bean stalks stood in their row. He had not thrown them away yet.

Mara pushed the parcel towards him. "The tap must have stuck. These should replace them." Ivo pushed it back. "I checked the tap. There was nothing wrong with it." She kept her hands beside the parcel instead of answering. Between them the string lay in a neat bow, still untied.

The greenhouse had grown close and breathless. Ivo's young tomatoes drooped towards the hot bench. He pulled the vent cord, but the cord parted and the pane stayed shut. Mara watched a leaf curl against the glass. "It has to stay open," Ivo said. "Not just while someone stands here holding it."

Mara tested the repair roll. Enough tape remained. Ivo held the vent up while she bound its handle to the upper bracket. She used the last length and set the empty roll down. When they let go, cooler air reached the tray. The parcel was still on the bench, its bow untouched; for once it had not been the answer.

Ivo gathered the beans from the parcel she opened and tipped them into Mara's cupped hands. "They are yours. I did not ask for replacements." She looked at the small hard shapes. "I helped, though." He nodded towards the vent. "That was help. It wasn't an answer about the tap."

Mara stepped outside, shut the door and walked back to the open gate with the beans in her hands. The empty waxed paper stayed on his bench. Ivo stayed by the greenhouse. She had brought something to leave behind and was carrying the important part away. At the gate she put the beans in her pocket, one careful handful at a time.

row.story:
Wind rattled the allotment greenhouse. Mara arrived with a waxed paper parcel of replacement beans. She had forgotten Ivo's watering, then blamed the tap. She wanted her friend back. At the gate she shifted the stone jamming its foot, pulled it open and carried the parcel up the path.

"Can I come in?" Mara asked. Ivo lifted his bucket away from the doorway. "Mind the latch." She opened the door, carried the parcel inside and put it on the dry bench before shutting the door. The dead bean stalks stood in their row. He had not thrown them away yet.

"The beans are for you," Mara said. Ivo left the string alone. "Did the shop have a tap too?" Her prepared excuses deserted her. "I forgot. The tap worked. Then I lied." He pressed a thumb into the bench soil. "I spent an hour taking it apart." This time she did not explain herself away.

A gust lifted the roof vent. Rain blew through the gap onto Ivo's young tomatoes, bending the matchstick stems. He pulled the closing cord; it came away in his hand. Mara caught the swinging end. Neither pull had moved the vent. "We need to hold it down," he said, looking up at the next cloud.

The tape roll was empty. Mara showed Ivo the cardboard centre, then asked for his sandwich tin. He opened it. She untied the parcel, tipped the beans into the tin, and spread the waxed paper across the gap and tied it against the vent handle with the parcel string. The tomatoes were sheltered now; her present had become a piece of the greenhouse.

Mara took the dry beans from the sandwich tin. Ivo moved six empty pots towards her and kept six for himself. "Only while I am here," he said. Mara nodded and stayed beside him. They pressed a bean into each pot. She left the soil loose this time, watching how lightly his fingers moved.

They stepped onto the path and Mara closed the door. Ivo kept the key. "Knock on Saturday." She nodded without asking for it. Through the glass stood twelve newly filled pots. There would be no coming and going on her own yet. She waited until he had finished speaking before turning towards the gate.

Mara tried to lift the tomato tray, but its rotten wooden base sagged. She set it back before it broke. As the heat curled the leaves, she slid her parcel under the bench instead. By the time she looked up, the stems had collapsed. The replacement beans were protected. Ivo's tomatoes were not.

There would be no coming and going on her own yet. She waited until he had finished speaking before turning towards the gate.

Sun glittered on the allotment greenhouse. Mara arrived with a waxed paper parcel of replacement beans. She had forgotten Ivo's watering, then blamed the tap. She wanted her friend back. At the gate she shifted the stone jamming its foot, pulled it open and carried the parcel up the path.

Their old measuring stick stood beside the door. Mara read the highest pencil mark: Ivo's initials, from a Sunday when the beans had grown without her. She touched the wood below it. Through the glass, he watched her hand. She let it fall without adding a mark of her own.

"Can I come in?" Mara asked. Ivo lifted his bucket away from the doorway. "Mind the latch." She opened the door, carried the parcel inside and put it on the dry bench before shutting the door. The dead bean stalks stood in their row. He had not thrown them away yet.

Mara pushed the parcel towards him. "The tap must have stuck. These should replace them." Ivo pushed it back. "I checked the tap. There was nothing wrong with it." She kept her hands beside the parcel instead of answering. Between them the string lay in a neat bow, still untied.

The greenhouse had grown close and breathless. Ivo's young tomatoes drooped towards the hot bench. He pulled the vent cord, but the cord parted and the pane stayed shut. Mara watched a leaf curl against the glass. "It has to stay open," Ivo said. "Not just while someone stands here holding it."

Mara tested the repair roll. Enough tape remained. Ivo held the vent up while she bound its handle to the upper bracket. She used the last length and set the empty roll down. When they let go, cooler air reached the tray. The parcel was still on the bench, its bow untouched; for once it had not been the answer.

Ivo gathered the beans from the parcel she opened and tipped them into Mara's cupped hands. "They are yours. I did not ask for replacements." She looked at the small hard shapes. "I helped, though." He nodded towards the vent. "That was help. It wasn't an answer about the tap."

Mara stepped outside, shut the door and walked back to the open gate with the beans in her hands. The empty waxed paper stayed on his bench. Ivo stayed by the greenhouse. She had brought something to leave behind and was carrying the important part away. At the gate she put the beans in her pocket, one careful handful at a time.

row.story:
Wind rattled the allotment greenhouse. Mara arrived with a waxed paper parcel of replacement beans. She had forgotten Ivo's watering, then blamed the tap. She wanted her friend back. At the gate she shifted the stone jamming its foot, pulled it open and carried the parcel up the path.

"Can I come in?" Mara asked. Ivo lifted his bucket away from the doorway. "Mind the latch." She opened the door, carried the parcel inside and put it on the dry bench before shutting the door. The dead bean stalks stood in their row. He had not thrown them away yet.

A snail was edging around an empty pot. Mara slipped a fallen leaf beneath it and set it in the big pot beside the doorway. Last summer they had called every snail Admiral. She nearly said it now. Ivo watched the leaf settle, but neither of them supplied the name.

"The beans are for you," Mara said. Ivo left the string alone. "Did the shop have a tap too?" Her prepared excuses deserted her. "I forgot. The tap worked. Then I lied." He pressed a thumb into the bench soil. "I spent an hour taking it apart." This time she did not explain herself away.

A gust lifted the roof vent. Rain blew through the gap onto Ivo's young tomatoes, bending the matchstick stems. He pulled the closing cord; it came away in his hand. Mara caught the swinging end. Neither pull had moved the vent. "We need to hold it down," he said, looking up at the next cloud.

The tape roll was empty. Mara showed Ivo the cardboard centre, then asked for his sandwich tin. He opened it. She untied the parcel, tipped the beans into the tin, and spread the waxed paper across the gap and tied it against the vent handle with the parcel string. The tomatoes were sheltered now; her present had become a piece of the greenhouse.

Mara took the dry beans from the sandwich tin. Ivo moved six empty pots towards her and kept six for himself. "Only while I am here," he said. Mara nodded and stayed beside him. They pressed a bean into each pot. She left the soil loose this time, watching how lightly his fingers moved.

They stepped onto the path and Mara closed the door. Ivo kept the key. "Knock on Saturday." She nodded without asking for it. Through the glass stood twelve newly filled pots. There would be no coming and going on her own yet. She waited until he had finished speaking before turning towards the gate.
